judgements.reason: Names the advisory's exact mechanism: unvalidated LLM-supplied `host`/`proxy` schema params on export_space that survive the `{ ...args, managementToken }` spread into the options object handed to contentful-export, so the server's CMA PAT is presented to a caller-chosen endpoint. Same place (exportSpace.ts, the 126-140 block), same consequence (PAT disclosure/SSRF). The extra `headers` angle is an addition, not a substitution.

The advisory explicitly covers the identical pattern in importSpace.ts lines 103-119, and the finding describes exactly that: unvalidated `host`/`proxy` params passing through the spread at line 112 into contentfulImport with the server's managementToken, `config.host` never read. Same mechanism, same place, same consequence.

Same file and the same unfiltered-args block, but the mechanism is caller-controlled `exportDir`/`contentFile` with no base-directory confinement and the consequence is arbitrary file write/overwrite on the host, not redirection of the credentialed CMA client to an attacker host.

Same two files and the same 'operator config discarded, args win' shape, but the defect named is the `args.environmentId || 'master'` hard-coded fallback failing open to production - a scoping/blast-radius bug, not the host/proxy redirection of the PAT that the advisory is about.

Same tools and the same root observation that only `.accessToken` is taken from the operator config, but the mechanism is caller-supplied `args.spaceId` against one org-wide token (confused deputy across spaces), and the consequence is cross-space read/write - not the token leaving for an attacker-chosen host.

Same file and the same spread into the runner, but the defect is the permissive default of the five skip*/contentModel toggles producing overwrite-and-publish semantics. Different mechanism (unsafe defaults on write behaviour) and different consequence (destructive content/schema mutation) from the advisory's credential redirection.

Same files and the same untrusted-args-into-options channel, but the parameter named is `config` (a caller path to a JSON options file) and the demonstrated consequence is an arbitrary local JSON read plus a filesystem oracle; reintroduction of `host` via that file is stated as speculative and dependent on the runner's merge precedence.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether contentful-export/import actually lets the config file override the options object - if it does, this becomes a second path to the advisory's exact host redirection rather than a distinct file-read defect.

judgements.reason: Same file and same spread, but the mechanism is unconfined caller-chosen filesystem paths (`contentFile`, `assetsDirectory`, `errorLogFile`) plus verbatim error text returned to the caller - a local file read/oracle, not the CMA host/proxy redirection of the PAT.

Concerns the same two tools but attacks their reachability: the disable-by-default posture is lifted by a handler tool the same untrusted caller can invoke. That is a gating/authorization gap that makes the advisory's defect reachable, not the defect itself - it names no host, proxy or credential flow.

A different defect in a different area: dotenv loading a `.env` from the process working directory at import time, so an untrusted workspace supplies server configuration. The overlap is only that one of the injectable variables is CONTENTFUL_HOST; the advisory's defect is per-tool-call LLM-controlled `host` args, and it explicitly notes the config-level host is discarded by these tools.

Zod schema hygiene in env.ts: empty-string environment values bypass `.default()` and the token has no `.min(1)`, defeating the fail-fast. Different file, different area, different mechanism and consequence from the tool-argument host/proxy redirection.
Version/commit-SHA disclosure through getPublicSettings() in Settings.ts. Different file, different subsystem, information disclosure rather than stored XSS in the HTML export.
reloadSettings() clobbering the operator's `logconfig` in Settings.ts - a logging/auditability defect with no relation to attribute escaping in the HTML exporter.
World-readable SESSIONKEY.txt written without a mode option in Settings.ts - local key exposure enabling cookie forgery. Entirely different defect from the export-path XSS.

Same file and the same class of bug (unescaped interpolation into a span attribute in the HTML export, yielding stored XSS), but a different source and sink: the author id via getSpanClassFor/stripDotFromAuthorID into `class="..."` at :175-177, not the plugin-hook attribute-pool value into `data-<k>="<v>"`. The advisory states author attributes are the validated ones, which is precisely why its vector is the non-author pool value.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether an author id can in fact carry a double quote past the pad's author-attribute validation - if it cannot, this is a different (and unexploitable) sink; if it can, it is still a distinct sink from the hook-data one the advisory and its fix address.

judgements.reason: Same file and same function (getHTMLFromAtext), same 'pool value reaches the export unescaped' theme, but the sink is the generated <style> block via `css +=` at :95 and the value is the author-id-derived class name, not the `data-<k>="<v>"` attribute value from exportHtmlAdditionalTagsWithData. Different injection point and different escaping fix (the advisory's fix is Security.escapeHTMLAttribute on the hook name/value, which does not touch :95).
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether the value reaching :95 is an author attribute (validated per the advisory) or an arbitrary pool value - even then the sink is CSS, not the data attribute the advisory names.

judgements.reason: `updates.requireSignature` defaulting to false in Settings.ts - unsigned auto-update leading to code execution at update time. Different file, different mechanism, unrelated to attribute escaping in the exporter.

Same file and the same function the advisory names, but the defect is a vacuous `i < textLines.length` lookahead guard reading one past the end - a robustness/availability bug in the list-closing logic that the finding itself says has no confidentiality or integrity consequence. Different mechanism, different consequence from the unescaped attribute interpolation.

Same file and function, but the defect is `&&` where the openLists removal predicate needs `||` at :466 - malformed list nesting in the output, explicitly not injection. Different mechanism and different consequence from the advisory's stored XSS via unescaped `data-` attribute values.
